evidence: createServer configures express(), express.json() and the route handlers: HTTP transport, which is an infrastructure responsibility.
Handlers only check that fields are present (e.g. `if (!id || !name) res.status(400)`): request-shape validation at the transport boundary.
Use-case work goes to taskService.createProject/addTask/assignTask/markTaskDone/listTasks in the application layer.
The error middleware `res.status(400).json({ error: error.message })` maps errors to HTTP responses: transport concern.
`dueDate ? new Date(dueDate) : undefined` is a type conversion of the request data, not a domain rule.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/server.ts handles HTTP transport only, and that is an infrastructure responsibility. createServer sets up the Express app, registers route handlers and adds an error-handling middleware. Each handler reads the request body, route params or query string. It checks that required fields are present (which is request-shape validation at the transport boundary, not a business rule), converts a few types (for example, dueDate to a Date) and passes the work to TaskService methods: createProject, createUser, addTask, assignTask, markTaskDone and listTasks. It then turns the results into HTTP status codes and JSON. No business rules are written here. Task state changes, assignment logic and filtering all live in the application service. The file also has no persistence logic of its own, because the repository is passed in from outside. It does create TaskService itself, but that is composition/wiring, which is acceptable at the infrastructure edge. Every error becomes a 400 response, which is a coarse choice, but it is still transport-level error mapping and not a responsibility that belongs to another layer.
